title: Identify common steel stock by sight and simple tests
mechanism_check: Stock shape decides how load flows: angle and channel resist bending along one axis, tube resists in all directions, flat bar is one-dimensional strength.
Mild steel is magnetic, dull gray, and cuts with a hacksaw steadily; stainless is magnetic-ish or not, shiny, and fights the saw; aluminum is light and non-magnetic.
A file bite test: a new file skates on hard steel, bites mild steel freely.
improvised_tools: A magnet from an old speaker or hard drive.
A mill file for the bite test.
A kitchen scale plus a tape measure: weigh a known length and compare to a steel-weight chart.
steps: Sort scrap by shape first: angle, tube/pipe, flat bar, round bar, sheet.
Test each pile with the magnet; separate non-magnetic aluminum for its own work.
File a hidden edge: free-biting means mild steel, skating means hard/high-carbon.
Weigh a measured length to estimate gauge or section size against a chart.
Label the rack before you forget what the test told you.
stop_conditions: PPE: cut edges slice like knives — gloves on whenever handling stock.
Stop: if you need certified alloy for a load-bearing part (trailers, hoists, structural frames), buy marked stock and get the welds inspected — scrap identification is not certification.
Stop: high-carbon or hardened steel (files skate) welds poorly without preheat and proper rod — treat as non-weldable scrap unless you know the alloy.

title: Read metal thickness by gauge without a gauge card
mechanism_check: Gauge is a backwards numbering system: bigger number means thinner metal; 16 gauge sheet is about 1.5 mm, 11 gauge about 3 mm.
Thickness decides the process: thin sheet welds with low amps or brazing, thick plate takes full-amp stick.
Stack comparison beats guessing: compare against a known reference coin or ruler edge.
improvised_tools: A steel ruler with mm markings — direct thickness reading.
A known reference: a US quarter is 1.75 mm thick, a penny 1.55 mm.
Calipers borrowed from anywhere beat every guess.
steps: Measure the metal with the ruler held square against the edge; read in mm.
Convert to gauge only when a chart or drawing demands it — mm is the truth.
Test weld heat on a scrap offcut of the same thickness first.
Choose the process by thickness: under 1.5 mm means tack-only, low-amp, or brazing.
Write the thickness on the piece with a marker before it joins the pile.
stop_conditions: PPE: sheet edges are razor wire — gloves and long sleeves.
Stop: thickness under 1 mm with a stick welder and no fine rod is a burn-through machine — switch to brazing, rivets, or sheet screws instead.
Stop: load-bearing parts need real measured thickness and a certified weld — guessing gauge is not engineering.

title: Mark and measure metal accurately with no scribe
mechanism_check: Accurate metalwork starts at layout: cut lines measured once with a bad mark ruin the piece.
A sharp steel point leaves a fine line a pencil cannot; the line is the datum every later step reads.
Measure from one end only (burn an inch is optional) so errors don't stack across marks.
improvised_tools: A hardened nail or awl as a scribe; a center punch or another nail for punch marks.
A combination square, speed square, or even a carpenter's square for right angles.
Soapstone or a lumber crayon — visible through cutting smoke and grinding dust.
steps: Clean the marking area to bare metal so the scribe bites.
Measure from one reference edge and scribe each mark with one firm pass.
Square every cross-line off the same reference edge.
Center-punch every hole location before drilling — the punch dimple starts the bit true.
Mark the waste side with an X so the saw never eats the part.
stop_conditions: PPE: gloves when handling sharp-marked sheet; the scribed edge plus the cut edge is a two-sided blade.
Stop: if the layout error stacks past 2 mm on a precision fit, re-mark from the datum instead of fudging the fit.
Stop: load-bearing assemblies need layout checked against the drawing, not eyeballed — stop and measure twice.

title: Deburr cut edges with improvised files
mechanism_check: Every cut leaves a burr — a raised, hardened lip that slices hands, blocks fit-up, and traps weld defects.
Burrs run along the cut edge in one direction; filing against the burr direction removes it, with the direction folds it over.
Two passes, not ten: a 45-degree chamfer pass, then one flat pass.
improvised_tools: Any mill or flat file; a round file for inside holes.
A sharpening stone or even a broken brick to knock down light burrs on sheet.
Emery cloth or sandpaper wrapped on a wood block for finish passes.
steps: Clamp the work so the edge faces you and both hands are free.
Push the file at 45 degrees along the edge in one direction — never saw back and forth.
Flip the piece and repeat the other side.
Run a bare fingertip (carefully) along the edge; any catch means another pass.
Wipe the edge clean before welding or paint.
stop_conditions: PPE: gloves while handling raw cut edges; safety glasses when filing hardened burrs that fling chips.
Stop: power-grinding a burr on thin sheet warps it — hand tools only under 1.5 mm.
Stop: a burr hiding a crack (not just a lip) is a different problem — inspect, don't file it smooth and weld over it.
Stop: deburring is prep, not repair — a burr hiding a crack in a load-bearing part needs inspection, not filing.

title: Clean metal to bare for welding without a grinder
mechanism_check: Welds fail on dirty metal: rust, mill scale, paint, and oil boil into the puddle and become porosity and cracks.
Clean metal is bright and reflective at least 20 mm back from the joint on both sides.
Chemical and abrasive cleaning both work; heat from welding is not a cleaner, it is a contaminant amplifier.
improvised_tools: A wire brush (hand or drill-mounted) plus elbow grease.
Sandpaper, emery cloth, or a flap disc on a drill.
Vinegar soak for heavy rust on small parts; acetone or degreaser for oil.
steps: Strip oil first with degreaser or acetone — rust removal on top of oil is wasted work.
Wire-brush the joint zone until it shines; check both faces and the edges.
For heavy rust, soak small parts in vinegar for a few hours, then brush.
Wipe with a clean dry rag right before tacking — flash rust starts fast on humid days.
Tack within the hour; cleaned steel re-oxidizes.
stop_conditions: PPE: gloves and eye protection; vinegar and degreasers are skin and eye irritants — ventilate.
Stop: never weld through paint, galvanizing, or plating to 'burn it off' — toxic fumes and guaranteed bad welds. Strip it or walk away.
Stop: if the cleaned metal shows pits deeper than 1 mm, the section is compromised — replace it rather than welding thin corroded plate.
Stop: load-bearing welds need a certified welder and inspection — cleaning the metal is prep, not qualification.

title: Clamp a square corner joint with no welding clamps
mechanism_check: A square joint is two faces held at 90 degrees under tacking; the enemy is movement during the tack, not the final weld.
Any right angle in the shop can act as the square: a machined block, a speed square, the corner of a flat table.
Clamping force must oppose the direction the heat will pull the joint — tack the inside corner first.
improvised_tools: C-clamps, bar clamps, or locking pliers (Vise-Grips) from the wood shop.
A carpenter's speed square or the corner of a steel table as the 90-degree reference.
Scrap angle iron bolted to a board as a reusable corner jig.
steps: Clean the joint faces to bare metal first — clamps won't fix dirty metal.
Butt the pieces against the square reference and check the gap is even.
Clamp so the force presses the pieces into the square, not just together.
Tack the inside of the corner first, then check square again before the second tack.
Let it cool fully before unclamping — hot steel relaxes and shifts.
stop_conditions: PPE: gloves; tacking throws spatter — hood and sleeves on even for a quick tack.
Stop: if the joint moves when you tack it, stop and re-clamp — welding a moved joint locks in the crooked.
Stop: load-bearing frames need the squareness checked after the full weld, not just the tacks — warping under full heat is real.

title: Improvise a magnetic square and tacking jig for steel joints
mechanism_check: A magnetic square holds thin steel at 90 degrees hands-free so both hands run the stinger.
Magnets work on mild steel only; stainless, aluminum, and hot steel ignore them.
The jig's job is repeatability: set it once, tack ten identical joints without re-measuring.
improvised_tools: Speaker or hard-drive magnets epoxied to two plates of scrap angle at 90 degrees.
Flat bar offcuts bolted into an L as a reusable corner fixture.
A steel table or plate as the flat reference plane.
steps: Glue or screw magnets to the faces of a scrap-angle L so both legs grip steel.
Test the jig against a known square before trusting it.
Set the workpieces into the jig, check the gap, and tack.
For repeats, clamp the jig itself to the bench so it can't wander.
Knock tacks loose with a hammer to free the jig — magnets pull free easily when cold.
stop_conditions: PPE: magnets pinch hard — keep fingers clear when they snap to steel; welding PPE still applies.
Stop: magnets lose pull near welding heat and arc interference — never trust a magnetic jig to hold a joint under full welding heat; it is a tacking aid only.
Stop: structural frames need hard clamping and post-weld square checks — magnets alone don't qualify.

title: Tack-weld basics: sequence and spacing for warp-free joints
mechanism_check: Tacks are temporary spot welds that freeze the fit-up before full welding; each tack shrinks as it cools and pulls the joint.
Tack from the center outward on long joints so shrinkage has somewhere to go.
More, smaller tacks beat fewer big ones: big tacks are just unwelded welds that crack.
improvised_tools: The same welder you will finish with, set 10-15% lower on amps.
Locking pliers and your square to re-check between tacks.
A ball-peen hammer to knock tacks back into alignment.
steps: Fit and clamp the joint, gap even along its length.
Place the first tack dead center, hold 2-3 seconds, release.
Check square, then tack outward toward each end, alternating sides.
Space tacks 25-50 mm apart on sheet, wider on thick plate.
Let the assembly cool, unclamp, verify square, then weld out.
stop_conditions: PPE: full arc PPE for tacks — hood, leather gloves, long sleeves; a 2-second tack still gives full arc flash.
Stop: cracked or cratered tacks must be ground out before the full weld — welding over a cracked tack buries the defect.
Stop: on load-bearing work, tacks are not the weld — the full weld plus inspection is the weld.

title: Set up a stick welder: amperage, polarity, and electrode choice
mechanism_check: Amperage sets heat: too low sticks and piles up, too high burns through and undercuts.
Electrode diameter sets the amp window: 2.5 mm rod runs 70-110 A, 3.2 mm runs 110-150 A, roughly 30-40 A per mm of rod.
6011/6010 dig deep and run dirty metal; 6013 is the forgiving all-rounder; 7018 is the strong, low-hydrogen rod that demands clean metal and dry storage.
improvised_tools: A scrap plate of the same thickness as the job for test beads.
A kitchen oven or sealed tube with desiccant to keep 7018 dry.
A file to dress a chipped electrode tip.
steps: Pick the rod: 6013 for general learning, 6011 for rusty farm work, 7018 for strong joints on clean metal.
Set amps to the middle of the rod's window for the thickness at hand.
Set polarity: DCEN (electrode negative) for thin and 6011 penetration control, DCEP (electrode positive) for deeper dig and 7018.
Run a test bead on scrap; adjust amps until the arc starts easily and the bead is flat, not crowned.
Write the winning setting on the machine with tape for next time.
stop_conditions: PPE: arc flash, spatter, and UV — hood, leather gloves, long sleeves, boots; bystanders need shielding too.
Stop: damp 7018 rods (left out overnight) cause hydrogen cracking in the weld — dry them or switch rods.
Stop: never weld on a closed container, tank, or drum — residual fuel or vapor turns it into a bomb. Purge and verify, or refuse the job.
Stop: machine setup is not qualification — load-bearing welds (trailers, hoists, structural frames) need a certified welder and inspection.

title: Set up a MIG welder: wire speed, voltage, and gas flow
mechanism_check: Voltage sets arc length and bead width; wire speed sets amperage (how much metal melts). They balance: raise one, raise the other.
Too little gas lets air in (porosity); too much gas wastes money and causes turbulence that also lets air in — 10-15 L/min covers most jobs.
Contact tip to work distance (stickout) runs 10-15 mm; longer stickout drops the effective amps.
improvised_tools: Scrap of job thickness for test beads.
A spare contact tip and nozzle — worn ones ruin everything.
Soapy water in a spray bottle to find gas leaks at fittings.
steps: Load the wire, set drive-roll tension so it feeds without bird-nesting.
Start with the machine's chart setting for the thickness; test-bead on scrap.
Listen: a steady bacon-sizzle is right; popping means too little wire, a harsh crackle means too much.
Set gas to 12 L/min and check the flow at the nozzle.
Spray fittings with soapy water; bubbles mean a leak to fix before welding.
stop_conditions: PPE: full arc PPE plus ventilation — MIG on painted or coated steel makes toxic fumes; respirator under the hood.
Stop: welding outdoors in wind blows the shielding gas away — build a windbreak or switch to flux-core/stick.
Stop: no gas, wrong gas, or empty bottle is not a 'weld anyway' situation — stop until shielding is restored.
Stop: machine setup is not qualification — load-bearing welds (trailers, hoists, structural frames) need a certified welder and inspection.

title: Strike and maintain an arc without sticking the rod
mechanism_check: The arc is a sustained spark across a 2-4 mm gap; the rod melts and the flux becomes shielding gas and slag.
Sticking happens when the gap closes: the rod fuses to the work and the machine hums — twist, don't yank.
Arc length controls everything: too long spatters and hisses, too short sticks and the bead piles up.
improvised_tools: Scrap plate for strike practice — never practice on the workpiece.
A striker's scratch pad: the corner of the ground clamp area starts arcs easier.
Pliers to snap a stuck rod free without burning your gloves.
steps: Set amps, clamp the ground close to the work on clean metal.
Strike like a match: scratch the rod across the plate and lift to a 3 mm gap.
Hold the gap steady and watch the puddle, not the arc flash.
Feed the rod down as it burns so the gap stays constant; move at puddle speed.
If it sticks, twist the holder sideways to break it free; file the tip and re-strike.
stop_conditions: PPE: auto-darkening hood, leather gloves, long sleeves, boots — arc flash hits bystanders too, so screen the area.
Stop: if the rod sticks repeatedly, amps are too low or the gap habit is off — adjust the machine, don't force it.
Stop: never strike an arc on the workpiece outside the joint — arc strikes are hard spots that crack.
Stop: striking arcs outside the joint on structural steel leaves hard spots that crack — and load-bearing welds need a certified welder and inspection.

title: Run a straight stringer bead on flat plate
mechanism_check: A stringer is a straight pass with no weave: the puddle should be roughly twice the rod diameter wide.
Travel speed sets bead shape: too fast gives a ropey, undercut bead; too slow gives a wide, sagging one.
The slag covering the bead is normal — it chips off to reveal the weld; don't weld over slag.
improvised_tools: Soapstone line on the plate as a travel guide.
A chipping hammer and wire brush for slag removal between passes.
Scrap plate for warm-up beads before the real joint.
steps: Scribe a straight guide line on the practice plate.
Strike the arc at the line's start and pause 2 seconds to build the puddle.
Travel along the line at the speed that keeps the puddle the right width.
Pause 2 seconds at the end to fill the crater, then break the arc sideways.
Chip the slag, brush clean, and read the bead: even ripples mean even speed.
stop_conditions: PPE: hood, leather gloves, sleeves; chipping slag needs eye protection — chips fly hot and sharp.
Stop: crater cracks at the bead end mean you rushed the finish — grind the crater out before the next pass.
Stop: structural welds need multi-pass technique and inspection, not a single pretty stringer.

title: Weld a tee joint: fit, tack sequence, and two-sided welding
mechanism_check: A tee is one plate standing on another; the fillet weld sits in the 90-degree corner on one or both sides.
One-sided tees bend under load; two-sided tees carry real force — know which the job needs.
Heat pulls the upright toward the welded side, so weld both sides in alternating passes to stay straight.
improvised_tools: Your corner jig or magnetic square from welding-007.
A wedge of scrap to hold the upright while tacking.
A level to verify the upright after each pass.
steps: Clean both faces, fit the upright square, clamp or jig it.
Tack the heel and toe of one side, check square, tack the other side.
Weld one side with a small fillet, let it cool, check square.
Weld the opposite side; the second pass pulls it back straight.
Chip, brush, and check both fillets for even legs and no undercut.
stop_conditions: PPE: full arc PPE; overhead-position tee welds throw spatter downward — add a leather bib.
Stop: undercut along the toe of a fillet on a load path is a crack starter — grind it out and re-weld.
Stop: tees in lifting, towing, or structural frames need a certified welder and inspection — this entry teaches the technique, not the qualification.

title: Weld a lap joint in thin sheet without burn-through
mechanism_check: Lap joints stack the sheets so the arc mostly plays on the top sheet's edge — the edge melts first and burns through fastest.
Thin sheet wants low heat and fast travel: many small tacks stitched together beat one continuous pass.
A copper or aluminum backing bar behind the joint soaks up excess heat and prevents blow-through.
improvised_tools: A copper pipe flattened as a heat-sink backing bar.
Sheet-metal screws or Clecos to hold the lap tight while stitching.
The lowest amp setting that still starts an arc reliably.
steps: Clean both sheets and clamp the lap tight — gaps are burn-through invitations.
Back the joint with the copper bar wherever you can reach.
Stitch: 15-20 mm tacks spaced apart, alternating ends toward the middle.
Let each stitch cool before the next; never run a continuous bead on thin lap.
Grind the stitches flush only if the surface must be flat; leave the crown otherwise.
stop_conditions: PPE: arc PPE plus fume control — thin sheet is often galvanized; zinc fumes demand a respirator and ventilation.
Stop: repeated burn-through means the process is wrong for the thickness — switch to brazing, rivets, or screws.
Stop: thin-sheet welds are cosmetic or light-duty only — never structural without engineering.

title: Control heat distortion on long seams
mechanism_check: Weld metal shrinks as it cools, pulling the joint toward the welded side — long seams bow, buckle, and twist.
Back-stepping (welding short segments from the finish end backward) spreads shrinkage evenly.
Tack heavily before welding: tacks every 25-50 mm are the cheapest distortion insurance.
improvised_tools: Heavy scrap as heat sinks clamped near the seam.
A straightedge to check flatness between passes.
A hammer and dolly for cold correction after welding.
steps: Tack the full seam at close spacing before any continuous welding.
Weld in back-step segments: 50-75 mm at a time, moving from the middle outward.
Alternate sides on double-sided joints; let each segment cool before the next.
Check flatness against the straightedge while the piece is still warm.
Correct minor bow cold with hammer and dolly; never hot-bend a fresh weld.
stop_conditions: PPE: full arc PPE; heavy plate stays hot long after the arc stops — mark hot work and let it cool.
Stop: quenching a weld with water to 'fix' distortion hardens and cracks it — air cool only.
Stop: precision-flat parts (machine beds, flanges) that must stay true need a professional with a press and heat plan — stop before you warp it beyond recovery.
Stop: distortion correction on structural members needs a professional heat-straightening plan — stop before you warp it beyond recovery.

title: Fix porosity: diagnose and re-weld a bad bead
mechanism_check: Porosity is trapped gas — visible as pinholes or wormholes in the bead; it kills weld strength.
Causes in order: dirty or wet metal, too-long arc, bad shielding gas coverage, damp rods.
A porous weld cannot be capped over — the defect stays buried and the cap cracks.
improvised_tools: A grinder or file to excavate the bad metal.
A wire brush and acetone for re-cleaning.
Dry rods from sealed storage to rule out moisture.
steps: Stop welding the moment porosity appears — continuing just buries more defects.
Grind the bad bead out completely until bright, sound metal shows.
Re-clean the joint: brush, degrease, verify gas flow and dry rods.
Shorten the arc and re-weld at the right heat.
Chip and inspect: no pinholes allowed before moving on.
stop_conditions: PPE: grinding PPE (face shield, glasses, respirator) plus arc PPE for the re-weld.
Stop: porosity through the full depth of a multi-pass weld means grinding out the whole joint — don't cap a defective root.
Stop: if a load-bearing weld keeps going porous, stop and get a certified welder — the base metal or procedure may be beyond DIY scope.

title: Grind a weld flush without gouging the parent metal
mechanism_check: Flush grinding blends the weld crown into the parent metal; gouging thins the parent and creates a stress notch.
The grinder cuts on its edge at a low angle — flat-on grinding digs craters, steep angles gouge.
Grind along the weld, not across it: across-the-weld passes leave a washboard.
improvised_tools: An angle grinder with a flap disc (less aggressive than a hard grinding wheel).
A straightedge to check flatness as you go.
Dykem or marker on the bead to see what you've touched.
steps: Mark the bead with marker so you can see your progress.
Grind along the bead at a shallow angle with light pressure — let the disc cut.
Check often with the straightedge; stop when the marker is gone and the surface is level.
Finish with a finer flap disc or hand file for a smooth blend.
Inspect for undercut at the toes — if you ground into the parent, the weld may need re-passing.
stop_conditions: PPE: face shield over safety glasses, gloves, respirator, hearing protection — grinders are the most dangerous shop tool.
Stop: sparks toward fuel, wood dust, or bystanders — set up spark shields and clear the area first.
Stop: never grind a structural weld flush to 'make it pretty' without knowing the weld's required throat size — thinning a structural fillet is structural damage.

title: Cut sheet metal with no shears
mechanism_check: Thin sheet cuts by shearing between two blades or by nibbling; the trick is supporting the waste side so it doesn't bend.
Score-and-snap works on thin soft sheet: a deep score line is a controlled tear path.
Power nibbling (drill-mounted nibbler) leaves the sheet flat where snips curl it.
improvised_tools: Aviation snips (straight, left, right) if any exist; otherwise a sharp cold chisel and hammer.
A drill plus a step bit for starting inside cuts.
A straight 2x4 clamped as a score guide for score-and-snap.
steps: Mark the line and the waste side; clamp the sheet flat to the bench.
For snips: cut with the waste curling away, long smooth strokes, not nibbles.
For score-and-snap: score deeply along the guide, clamp the line at the bench edge, snap downward.
For inside cutouts: drill a starter hole, then work outward with snips or chisel.
Deburr every edge immediately — fresh sheet edges are razor wire.
stop_conditions: PPE: heavy gloves and eye protection; sheet edges and flying snip chips are both cutters.
Stop: sheet over 1.5 mm with hand snips is hand-injury territory — switch to a jigsaw with a metal blade or a chisel.
Stop: never cut sheet that may be galvanized with heat (grinder/plasma) without a respirator — zinc fume hazard.
Stop: cut edges on load-bearing sheet reduce the section — get the design checked before cutting structural panels.

title: Cut steel rod and bar with no bandsaw
mechanism_check: Steel rod cuts by abrasion (hacksaw, grinder cutoff wheel) or by shear (bolt cutters on soft small rod).
A hacksaw cuts on the push stroke with the blade tensioned tight; loose blades wander and break.
Wrapping tape around the cut line keeps the saw from skating and marks square all around.
improvised_tools: A hacksaw with a fresh 18-24 TPI bimetal blade.
Tape wrapped around the bar as a square guide.
A V-block of wood with a notch to cradle round bar while sawing.
steps: Wrap tape around the bar at the cut line; scribe square on the tape.
Seat the bar in the V-block and clamp it — never hand-hold.
Start the cut with light pull strokes to establish the kerf.
Saw with long, steady push strokes; let the blade cut, don't bear down.
File the cut face flat and deburr the edges before use.
stop_conditions: PPE: gloves and eye protection; broken hacksaw blades snap sharp.
Stop: hardened steel (files skate) will destroy blades — anneal it or use an abrasive cutoff wheel.
Stop: cutoff wheels on grinders need the guard on and the wheel rated above the grinder's RPM — a bursting wheel is shrapnel.
Stop: cut stock for load-bearing use must be known alloy and grade — mystery bar is not structural material.

title: Drill metal with no drill press
mechanism_check: A drill bit cuts with its two lips; wandering starts when the chisel point skates on hard metal — the center-punch dimple is the fix.
Small pilot hole first, then step up: a big bit grabbing in thin metal spins the workpiece.
Cutting oil keeps the bit cool; a smoking bit is a dying bit.
improvised_tools: A hand drill and sharp bits; a center punch for starting dimples.
Cutting oil, or motor oil in a pinch, dripped on the cut.
A wood block with a V-notch or a clamped angle to cradle round stock.
steps: Center-punch every hole location — no punch, no accuracy.
Clamp the work solid; never hand-hold metal being drilled.
Start with a pilot hole 1/3 the final diameter.
Step up in two or three bits, oiling each pass, moderate speed and firm pressure.
Deburr both sides of the hole immediately.
stop_conditions: PPE: eye protection — metal chips are hot and sharp; gloves off near rotating bits (glove-catch spins hands into the chuck).
Stop: if the bit grabs and spins the workpiece, release the trigger and re-clamp — a spinning steel plate is a blade.
Stop: drilling hardened steel with normal bits just ruins bits — anneal the spot or use cobalt bits at slow speed.
Stop: holes in structural members need engineering — drilling a beam flange or lifting lug without a plan weakens it.

title: Straighten bent steel bar with no press
mechanism_check: Bending stretches the outside of the bend and compresses the inside; straightening reverses it by working the stretched side.
Cold straightening with a hammer works the high spot down; heat straightening uses a rosebud to shrink the stretched fibers.
Work in small corrections and check often — over-correcting starts a new bend the other way.
improvised_tools: A heavy hammer and a flat anvil surface (sledge head, rail section, thick plate).
Two wood blocks as fulcrums for three-point bending by hand or with a jack.
A straightedge to check progress.
steps: Mark the high spot of the bend with soapstone.
Support the bar on blocks straddling the bend.
Hammer the high spot with controlled blows, or press with a bottle jack between fixed points.
Check with the straightedge after every few blows.
Flip and repeat for S-bends; finish with light passes to smooth hammer marks.
stop_conditions: PPE: eye protection and gloves — hammer-on-steel throws chips; secure the work so it can't kick.
Stop: cracked or kinked bar (sharp crease, not a smooth bend) is weakened — replace it, don't straighten it.
Stop: straightening heat-treated or load-rated parts (axles, tow bars, jack handles) destroys their temper — replace, never re-bend.
Stop: straightened bar is never as strong as new — never use re-straightened stock for load-bearing parts.

title: Straighten bent sheet with hammer and dolly
mechanism_check: Sheet dents are stretched metal; hammering on-dolly (hammer directly over the dolly) compresses the stretch back down.
Off-dolly work raises low spots; on-dolly work lowers high spots — pick the right one for the dent.
Light, fast taps move sheet; heavy blows stretch it worse.
improvised_tools: A body hammer or ball-peen; a dolly improvised from a smooth sledge head or a section of rail.
A sandbag or leather shot bag as a soft dolly for curved panels.
A straightedge and raking light to read the surface.
steps: Read the dent in raking light and mark the high and low areas.
Back the high spot with the dolly and tap on-dolly with light blows.
Work from the outside of the dent inward — chasing the center first stretches it.
Check in raking light often; stop when it reads flat.
File or sand lightly to blend hammer marks.
stop_conditions: PPE: eye protection and gloves; clamp or hold the sheet so it can't slip and guillotine fingers.
Stop: cracked or torn sheet at the dent is not a straightening job — patch or replace it.
Stop: sheet thinner than 1 mm work-hardens fast and tears — switch to shrinking or replacement.
Stop: straightened sheet has work-hardened zones — not for structural panels or load-bearing skins.

title: Bend sheet metal with no brake
mechanism_check: Sheet bends along a line when the outside fibers stretch past yield; a sharp inside edge (angle iron) defines the bend line.
Bend allowance: the bend consumes a little extra material at the radius — sharp bends crack, generous radii survive.
Clamp the bend line hard; the bend forms at the clamp edge, nowhere else.
improvised_tools: Two pieces of angle iron or a 2x4 sandwich clamped along the bend line.
A rubber mallet or wood block and hammer for forming.
A protractor or angle finder to check the bend.
steps: Mark the bend line and clamp the sheet between the angles exactly on it.
Start the bend with hand pressure, working from the center outward.
Tap the flange down with the mallet, progressing along the line.
Check the angle; over-bend slightly — sheet springs back a few degrees.
Relieve sharp inside corners with a file to prevent cracking.
stop_conditions: PPE: gloves — the bent flange edge is a blade; eye protection for mallet work.
Stop: sheet thicker than 2 mm or wider than your clamps won't bend cleanly by hand — find a shop with a brake.
Stop: bending across existing welds or hardened zones cracks — anneal first or re-plan the bend location.
Stop: hand-bent brackets are light-duty — load-bearing brackets need engineered design and certified welds.

title: Bend tubing with no bender (sand-packed method)
mechanism_check: Tube kinks when the inside wall collapses under compression; packing it with sand makes the cross-section incompressible.
The bend forms around a radius form — tighter than 3x the tube diameter kinks even packed tube.
Cap both ends tight or the sand escapes and the kink wins.
improvised_tools: Dry fine sand packed hard into the tube; wood plugs or crimped ends as caps.
A radius form: a pulley, a drum, or a plywood disc of the right radius.
A long cheater pipe slipped over the tube for leverage.
steps: Dry the sand completely (damp sand steams and blows caps off if heated).
Pack the tube in short lifts, tamping each hard; cap both ends tight.
Mark the bend start and clamp the tube to the radius form.
Pull steadily with the cheater — one smooth motion, no jerking.
Uncap, pour out the sand, and check the bend against a template.
stop_conditions: PPE: gloves and eye protection; a slipping cheater pipe swings hard — keep the swing zone clear.
Stop: never heat packed tube to bend it — steam pressure can blow the caps like a gun.
Stop: thin-wall or structural tube (roll cages, handrails) bent this way is cosmetic-grade — load-bearing bends need a proper mandrel bender.

title: Remove heavy rust with no power tools
mechanism_check: Rust is iron oxide with no strength; removal is mechanical (wire brush, abrasive) or chemical (acid converts or dissolves it).
Vinegar and citric acid dissolve rust slowly and safely; phosphoric-acid converters turn rust into a paintable black layer.
Rust hides pits — the metal under heavy scale is thinner than it looks, so measure after cleaning.
improvised_tools: Hand wire brush and a drill-mounted wire wheel if a drill exists.
White vinegar or citric acid solution for soaking small parts.
Naval jelly or phosphoric-acid rust converter for large surfaces.
steps: Knock off loose scale with the wire brush first.
Soak small parts in vinegar 4-12 hours, then scrub; or brush converter onto large areas.
Rinse and dry immediately — bare steel flash-rusts in minutes.
Measure the remaining thickness; pits deeper than 1 mm mean replacement.
Prime or oil the surface the same day.
stop_conditions: PPE: gloves and eye protection; acids burn skin and eyes — ventilate and keep baking soda handy to neutralize.
Stop: rust that has perforated the section is not restorable — cut it out and patch or replace.
Stop: structural members with heavy section loss need a certified evaluation, not a wire brush.

title: Cut a bolt or rod straight with a hacksaw
mechanism_check: Threads are the guide: clamping the bolt by its unthreaded shank in a vise protects the threads.
A nut threaded on before the cut and run off after cleans the burr and restores the thread start.
Cut square or the fastener seats crooked and loads one side.
improvised_tools: A vise or locking pliers clamping the shank.
A sacrificial nut threaded onto the bolt before cutting.
A file to chamfer the cut end.
steps: Thread a nut onto the bolt past the cut line.
Clamp the shank in the vise, cut line just proud of the jaws.
Saw square with steady push strokes; keep the blade 90 degrees.
Back the nut off over the cut end to chase the threads clean.
File a small chamfer so the bolt starts easily.
stop_conditions: PPE: gloves and eye protection; a snapping blade throws shards.
Stop: hardened bolts (grade 8, socket-head) eat hacksaw blades — use an abrasive wheel or buy the right length.
Stop: never cut a bolt under tension or a loaded fastener — unload the joint first.
Stop: a cut bolt loses its grade marking and heat treat at the cut — never use a cut bolt as a graded, load-bearing fastener.

title: Extract a broken bolt from steel
mechanism_check: A broken bolt is held by corrosion and thread friction; the extractor's job is to bite and turn, not to drill the bolt out completely.
Left-hand drill bits often spin the stub out by themselves — the extractor is plan B.
Heat breaks the corrosion bond: the bolt expands, breaks the rust seal, then contracts looser.
improvised_tools: Left-hand drill bits and a screw extractor set.
Penetrating oil (or ATF mixed with acetone).
A propane torch for heat-cycling the area around the bolt.
steps: Soak the stub in penetrating oil; tap it lightly to help the oil wick in.
Center-punch the stub dead center and drill a pilot hole with the left-hand bit.
If the stub backs out on the drill, done — chase the threads and move on.
Otherwise tap the extractor in firmly and turn it out with a tap wrench, slow and square.
If the extractor snaps, stop — hardened extractor steel needs a professional with EDM or a carbide setup.
stop_conditions: PPE: eye protection for drilling; gloves for torch work; ventilate — penetrating oil smokes and flames.
Stop: a snapped extractor inside the bolt is beyond DIY — hardened steel can't be drilled with normal bits; take it to a machine shop.
Stop: never weld a nut to a bolt stub inside an aluminum part or near fuel — heat and spatter where they don't belong.
Stop: an extracted-and-repaired hole in a load-bearing part needs professional evaluation — the threads are compromised.

title: Repair stripped threads with no tap set
mechanism_check: Stripped threads are deformed, not gone — a thread chaser or the right bolt can often reform them.
Oversize-and-retap is the honest fix; thread inserts (Heli-Coil style) restore the original size in soft metal.
A nut welded over a stripped hole is a last-resort farm fix, not a precision repair.
improvised_tools: The correct bolt plus cutting oil to chase threads gently.
A thread file for cleaning up external threads.
A Heli-Coil or threaded-insert kit for the proper fix in aluminum or thin steel.
steps: Try chasing first: oil the hole, run the correct bolt in by hand, back it out often.
If chasing fails, drill to the insert kit's specified size and install the insert per its instructions.
For steel plate, drilling oversize and tapping the next size up is the durable fix.
Test with a fresh bolt — it should thread by hand for the first turns.
Never force a cross-threaded start; back out and re-align.
stop_conditions: PPE: eye protection for drilling; gloves for sharp drilled edges.
Stop: stripped threads in a safety-critical fastener (suspension, brakes, lifting) get replaced or professionally repaired — no improvised fixes.
Stop: drilling oversize in thin material leaves too little meat — switch to a through-bolt with a nut instead.
Stop: repaired threads are weaker than original — never trust them in lifting, structural, or load-bearing joints.

title: Brazing basics: join steel with a torch and bronze rod
mechanism_check: Brazing doesn't melt the base metal — bronze filler melts around 870 C and flows into the joint by capillary action.
The joint must be tight (0.05-0.15 mm gap) and surgically clean; flux dissolves oxides so the bronze wets the steel.
Heat the metal, not the rod: the hot base metal melts the rod on contact — that proves the joint is hot enough.
improvised_tools: A propane or MAPP torch for small joints; oxy-fuel for bigger ones.
Bronze brazing rod with matching flux.
Firebricks or a steel plate to reflect heat back into small parts.
steps: Clean the joint to bright metal and fit it tight; flux both faces.
Heat the joint evenly until the flux turns clear and glassy.
Touch the rod to the joint — if it melts on contact, the temperature is right; feed sparingly.
Let capillary action pull the bronze in; don't glob rod on top.
Let it cool naturally, then wire-brush the glassy flux residue off.
stop_conditions: PPE: shade-3 to shade-5 glasses for torch work, leather gloves, long sleeves; fire extinguisher within reach.
Stop: brazing near fuel lines, gas tanks, or sealed containers — purge and verify or refuse.
Stop: brazed joints are strong but not fusion welds — never braze lifting, towing, or structural joints and call them welded.

title: Solder heavy copper and steel lugs with no soldering iron
mechanism_check: Heavy lugs need mass heat — a torch or a heated bolt does what an iron can't.
Solder flows toward heat, so heat the lug body and let the solder wick into the joint.
Flux is mandatory on copper: without it the solder balls up and rolls off.
improvised_tools: A propane torch or a large bolt heated in a fire as a soldering copper.
Rosin or plumbing flux and electrical solder.
A vise or pliers to hold the hot lug.
steps: Clean the wire and lug to bright metal; flux both.
Clamp the lug so the wire stays put without your hands near the heat.
Heat the lug body until flux sizzles, then touch solder to the joint — not to the flame.
Feed until solder wicks through and shows at the far side.
Hold still until it freezes; a moved joint crystallizes and fails.
stop_conditions: PPE: leather gloves and eye protection — molten solder spatters; work over a fire-safe surface.
Stop: soldered joints carry current, not load — never solder a mechanical joint and trust it structurally.
Stop: acid plumbing flux on electronics corrodes the joint — use rosin flux for electrical work.

title: Cold-join a bracket with rivets and no rivet gun
mechanism_check: A rivet is a permanent pin: the shop head forms on the blind side and clamps the stack by upsetting.
Solid rivets need bucking (a heavy mass behind the head); pop rivets need only the hand tool.
Hole fit matters: 0.1-0.2 mm clearance; sloppy holes make sloppy joints.
improvised_tools: Pop rivets and a hand riveter, or solid rivets with a ball-peen hammer.
A sledge head or heavy steel block as a bucking bar.
Drill bits matched to the rivet diameter.
steps: Drill the stack together so the holes align; deburr both sides.
For pop rivets: insert, squeeze the tool until the stem snaps.
For solid rivets: insert from the finished side, back the head with the bucking bar, and peen the tail into a shop head.
Check each rivet: the head should be tight to the surface with no gap.
Seal outdoor rivets with paint or sealant to stop crevice corrosion.
stop_conditions: PPE: eye protection — snapped pop-rivet stems fly; gloves for sharp drilled edges.
Stop: rivets are single-shear fasteners — never substitute rivets for welds on a joint designed as welded and load-bearing.
Stop: aluminum rivets in steel without isolation corrode galvanically — use coated or stainless rivets outdoors.

title: Improvise a nut from flat stock with drill and file
mechanism_check: A nut is a threaded block; the thread does the work and the hex is just a wrench interface.
A square or round improvised nut works if the thread engagement is at least one bolt diameter deep.
Without a tap, a drilled hole plus a thread-cutting bolt can form usable threads in soft steel.
improvised_tools: Flat bar offcuts, a drill, and files.
A hardened bolt of the target thread as a forming tap, with cutting oil.
A vise to hold the work while threading.
steps: Cut a flat-bar square at least 2x the bolt diameter across and as thick as the bolt diameter.
Drill the tap-drill size hole (roughly bolt diameter minus pitch).
Oil the hole and drive the hardened bolt in a half-turn at a time, backing out to clear chips.
File two flats or a hex on the outside for a wrench to grab.
Test on a fresh bolt — it should turn with firm hand resistance, not slop.
stop_conditions: PPE: eye protection for drilling and filing; clamp the work — never hand-hold.
Stop: improvised nuts are for low-load, non-critical joints only — buy real graded nuts for anything that matters.
Stop: never improvise a nut for a high-vibration or safety joint — it will back off or strip.
Stop: improvised nuts are for low-load, non-critical joints only — never use one in a structural or safety-critical fastener.

title: Repurpose scrap steel into brackets and hooks
mechanism_check: Scrap already has shape and strength — the job is seeing the bracket inside the offcut.
Bends concentrate stress at the inside corner; a small gusset or a generous radius doubles the bracket's life.
Hooks want a closed or curled end so loads can't walk off.
improvised_tools: Scrap angle, flat bar, and tube offcuts.
Your bending setup from welding-023 and drilling from welding-020.
Bolts or rivets from welding-031 for assembly.
steps: Sort scrap by usable shape and sketch the bracket to fit the stock, not the reverse.
Cut and bend the blank; drill mounting holes before bending.
Close hook ends with a curl or a welded/bolted keeper.
Deburr everything — shop-made brackets get handled constantly.
Paint or oil the finished piece; bare scrap rusts from handling.
stop_conditions: PPE: gloves and eye protection through cutting, bending, and drilling.
Stop: scrap of unknown alloy or with cracks is decoration-grade — don't hang loads on mystery metal.
Stop: brackets that are load-bearing or hold people, engines, or overhead loads need engineered design and certified welds — scrap improvisation doesn't qualify.

title: Build a welding cart from scrap
mechanism_check: A cart is a low, stable frame: wide wheelbase, low center of gravity, the bottle chained upright.
The welder sits low, cables hang on hooks, the bottle rides at the back chained at two points.
Everything bolted or welded square — a wobbling cart plus a gas bottle is a falling hazard.
improvised_tools: Scrap angle or tube for the frame, casters or wheels from anything rolling.
Chain or a ratchet strap to secure the bottle.
Your tacking jig from welding-007 for square assembly.
steps: Sketch the footprint: welder shelf low, bottle bay at the back, handle at the front.
Cut and tack the frame square; verify diagonals match before full welding.
Mount the bottle bay with chain anchors at two heights.
Add caster plates, cable hooks, and a rod tube from scrap pipe.
Load-test it empty first: shove it hard — any wobble gets a gusset.
stop_conditions: PPE: full arc PPE for the frame welds; grinding PPE for cleanup.
Stop: the gas bottle must be chained upright at all times — a falling bottle can shear its valve and become a rocket.
Stop: the cart carries the welder, not the qualification — frame welds are light-duty, fine; don't hang a shop crane off it.
Stop: the cart frame is light-duty — never hang load-bearing equipment (chain hoists, shop cranes) from it.

title: Build a welding table surface from scrap plate
mechanism_check: A welding table is a flat, thick, grounded steel top: thick enough to take tack spatter and clamp abuse without warping.
3/8 inch (10 mm) plate stays flat under hobby heat; thinner tops oil-can and warp.
The ground clamp bites the table, so the top must be bare steel, not painted.
improvised_tools: The thickest scrap plate you can find, plus angle or tube legs.
A straightedge to verify flatness.
Clamps to hold the top flat while tacking the legs.
steps: Check the plate for flatness with the straightedge; reject oil-canned plate.
Cut legs and tack the frame, keeping the top clamped flat.
Weld the legs with alternating passes to avoid pulling the top.
Grind the top to bare metal; leave it unpainted — spatter and ground need steel.
Add a lower shelf for clamps and a ground-clamp tab.
stop_conditions: PPE: full arc and grinding PPE; plate edges are heavy and sharp — get help lifting.
Stop: never use a flammable or wooden top as a 'welding table' — sparks and slag set it alight.
Stop: a table is a work surface, not a press or an anvil stand — don't beat work into shape on a thin top.
Stop: the table is a work surface, not a structural frame — don't use it as a press or load-bearing support.

title: Improvise welding ventilation and fume extraction in a garage
mechanism_check: Welding fume is vaporized metal and flux — manganese, zinc, and hex-chrome depending on the metal; the dose makes the poison.
Dilution (big airflow) plus capture (fume pulled at the arc) beats either alone.
Your head position matters most: never weld with your face in the rising plume.
improvised_tools: A box fan in the window blowing OUT, plus a cracked door or second window for make-up air.
A cheap inline duct fan with flex hose positioned near the arc as a capture hood.
A P100 half-face respirator that fits under the hood.
steps: Set the exhaust fan to pull air across the work and out, not to blow across the arc (wind ruins MIG gas).
Position the capture hose 30-45 cm from the arc, on the downwind side.
Keep your head out of the visible plume — reposition the work, not your lungs.
Wear the respirator for galvanized, stainless, or painted steel, no exceptions.
Change the airflow check each session: a ribbon taped near the arc should stream toward the exhaust.
stop_conditions: PPE: respirator under the hood for coated metals; the hood alone is not fume protection.
Stop: welding galvanized or stainless indoors with no extraction and no respirator — walk away until both exist.
Stop: never weld in a sealed room 'for a quick tack' — fume dose accumulates and you can't smell the worst of it.
Stop: fume control doesn't qualify a weld — load-bearing welds still need a certified welder and inspection.

title: Set up a safe welding station: power, ground, and fire watch
mechanism_check: A welder is a high-current device on a normal circuit: the breaker, the extension cord gauge, and the duty cycle all have to agree.
The ground clamp completes the circuit through the workpiece — a bad ground makes the arc wander and heats the clamp.
Sparks travel 10 meters and smolder for an hour: fire watch is a person with an extinguisher, not a hope.
improvised_tools: The shortest, heaviest extension cord available (12 AWG minimum for 120 V welders).
A dedicated circuit if possible; know which breaker feeds your outlet.
A fire extinguisher, a bucket of water, and a 30-minute post-weld watch timer.
steps: Plug the welder directly into the outlet or the shortest heavy cord — coiled cords overheat.
Clamp the ground to clean, bare metal on the workpiece or the steel table.
Clear 10 meters of combustibles; sweep the floor — sparks find sawdust.
Set out the extinguisher and water; designate the fire watcher.
After welding, watch the area 30 minutes — smoldering starts long after the arc stops.
stop_conditions: PPE: full arc PPE before the first test strike; fire watch stays suited while sparks fly.
Stop: breakers tripping repeatedly means the circuit is overloaded — stop and get a proper circuit, don't bypass the breaker.
Stop: never weld within 10 meters of fuel, solvents, or gas bottles without moving them first — no exceptions.
Stop: a safe station doesn't certify the welds made in it — load-bearing work needs a certified welder and inspection.

title: Why thin aluminum is a stop without the right setup
mechanism_check: Aluminum conducts heat away six times faster than steel and melts with no color warning — it goes from solid to puddle instantly.
Its oxide layer melts at 2000 C while the metal melts at 660 C: without AC TIG or a spool gun, you weld oxide, not aluminum.
Thin aluminum with a stick or plain MIG setup is a burn-through and porosity factory.
improvised_tools: A spool gun or push-pull MIG setup as the minimum viable aluminum tool.
Stainless wire brush dedicated to aluminum only (steel contamination ruins it).
Acetone for cleaning — aluminum must be surgically clean.
steps: Assess the job: under 3 mm aluminum without a spool gun or TIG is a no-go — choose rivets, bolts, or adhesive.
If equipped: clean with the dedicated stainless brush, wipe with acetone.
Preheat thick sections gently; weld fast and hot — lingering causes burn-through.
Expect to practice on scrap first; aluminum punishes every hesitation.
Inspect for the tell-tale black soot of a contaminated weld — grind it out and redo.
stop_conditions: PPE: full arc PPE; aluminum welding fumes and UV are both aggressive — respirator recommended.
Stop: thin aluminum with a stick welder or plain MIG is not a skill issue, it's a physics issue — stop and change process or fastener.
Stop: structural aluminum (trailers, marine, aircraft) needs certified procedures and inspection — never DIY.

title: Weld a cracked cast-iron bracket: preheat and nickel rod
mechanism_check: Cast iron is high-carbon and brittle: welding heat creates a hard, crack-prone zone unless the whole part is preheated.
Nickel rod (Ni55/Ni99) stays ductile and tolerates the carbon migration that cracks steel-rod welds on cast iron.
Slow cooling is the whole game — fast cooling re-hardens the weld zone and it cracks overnight.
improvised_tools: Nickel 55 rod and a propane weed burner or oven for preheat.
A temperature-indicating crayon or an IR thermometer.
Dry sand, a bucket of vermiculite, or a welding blanket for slow cooling.
steps: V-groove the crack fully — a surface skim weld on cast iron always fails.
Preheat the whole part to 250-300 C, evenly, not just the joint.
Weld short 25 mm beads with nickel rod, peening each bead lightly while hot to relieve stress.
Bury the part in sand or wrap it in the blanket immediately — cool over hours, not minutes.
Inspect the next day: tap-test and dye-check if available; any new crack means re-do or replace.
stop_conditions: PPE: full arc PPE plus heat PPE — preheated cast iron burns through gloves; long sleeves and face protection.
Stop: cast iron that is oil-soaked (engine blocks) or previously brazed needs professional evaluation — contamination defeats the weld.
Stop: safety-critical cast parts (brake components, steering, lifting lugs) are replace-don't-weld — no DIY exceptions.
Stop: any cast-iron repair in a load-bearing or safety-critical role needs a certified welder and inspection — this entry covers the technique, not the qualification.

title: Build a metal gate frame from tube stock
mechanism_check: A gate is a rectangle that wants to become a parallelogram: the diagonal brace is what keeps it square.
Hinge-side load is cantilevered — the frame's hinge stile carries the whole gate's weight times the lever arm.
Weld sequence decides whether it hangs true: tack everything, check square, then weld alternating sides.
improvised_tools: Square tube stock, hinges, and a latch.
A flat driveway or floor as the assembly reference plane.
Diagonal measuring tape: equal diagonals mean square.
steps: Cut all four sides; miter or cope the corners for full weld contact.
Lay out on the flat reference, tack the rectangle, check diagonals equal.
Tack the diagonal brace from the bottom hinge corner to the top latch corner.
Weld out with alternating passes; re-check diagonals while warm.
Hang with the hinges on the braced corner side; shim until it swings free and latches.
stop_conditions: PPE: full arc and grinding PPE; tube ends are sharp — deburr before handling.
Stop: gates over vehicles or where failure injures people need engineered hinges and posts — a garden gate is DIY, a driveway gate over a sidewalk is not.
Stop: if the frame twists during weld-out and won't come back square, cut the tacks and re-fit — forcing a twisted gate straight never holds.
Stop: gates that guard drops, retain vehicles, or carry structural loads need engineered design and certified welds — a garden gate is DIY, a structural gate is not.

title: Run a five-minute fit-up review before striking an arc
mechanism_check: Most weld defects are fit-up defects: gaps, misalignment, and dirty metal decided before the arc starts.
A five-minute review catches what an hour of welding can't fix — the review is cheaper than the rework.
The reviewer needs fresh eyes: the person who fit the joint shouldn't be the only one who checks it.
improvised_tools: A checklist on a shop whiteboard or taped to the welder: clean, gap, square, clamp, ground.
A second pair of eyes — even an apprentice can run the checklist.
A straightedge and square at the review station.
steps: Stop before the first arc and walk the checklist: clean metal, even gap, square, clamps tight, ground on bare metal.
Measure diagonals on frames; check hole alignment on bolted-welded assemblies.
The reviewer initials the checklist — ownership makes it real.
Fix every finding before welding, not during.
Log repeat findings; the same miss twice means the checklist needs a new line.
stop_conditions: PPE: the review happens cold, but the fix-up may involve grinding — eye protection and gloves on.
Stop: if the fit-up can't be made right, stop — welding a bad fit-up to 'make it work' is how structural failures start.
Stop: load-bearing assemblies that fail review go to a certified welder or engineer, not to a re-weld.

title: Mentor an apprentice welder: teach the puddle first
mechanism_check: Beginners watch the arc; welders watch the puddle — the skill transfer is a change of attention, not just technique.
Short, frequent coached reps beat long unsupervised practice: bad habits weld themselves in within a day.
The mentor's job is narration: saying what they see teaches the apprentice what to look at.
improvised_tools: Scrap plate and a dedicated practice station the apprentice can use without interrupting production.
A spare hood so the mentor can watch the apprentice's puddle directly.
A simple progression card: strike arc, run straight, tee joint, then real work.
steps: Demonstrate one bead while narrating what the puddle is doing — speed, width, color.
Let the apprentice run beads on scrap while you watch the puddle, not their hands.
Correct one thing at a time: arc length first, then travel speed, then angle.
Promote to real joints only when scrap beads are consistent; start them on tacks.
Review their welds together weekly — the review teaches judgment, not just hands.
stop_conditions: PPE: apprentice gets full arc PPE from day one — no 'just watch' without a hood.
Stop: if the apprentice keeps striking arcs on the workpiece or skipping PPE, pull them back to scrap until the habits are safe.
Stop: apprentices don't weld load-bearing joints unsupervised — certified oversight stays mandatory.

title: Lay out a one-person fab shop for flow: cut, fit, weld, finish
mechanism_check: A shop is a production line bent into a room: material should move cut → fit → weld → finish without backtracking.
Every backtrack is wasted motion and a chance to damage finished work with sparks and grinding dust.
Zones beat piles: a defined zone for each stage keeps hot work away from finished work.
improvised_tools: Tape on the floor or chalk lines to mark the four zones.
Rolling carts or sawhorses so work moves between zones without carrying.
A welding screen or curtain separating the weld zone from fit and finish.
steps: Mark four zones in sequence: cutting, fit-up, welding, finishing — in the order work actually flows.
Put the welder, ground, and fume extraction permanently in the weld zone.
Keep grinders in finishing, never in fit-up — grinding dust in a fit-up joint becomes weld porosity.
Stage material at the cutting zone entrance and finished work at the finishing zone exit.
Re-walk the flow monthly; shops drift back into piles without the ritual.
stop_conditions: PPE: zone separation doesn't replace PPE — full arc and grinding PPE in the right zones.
Stop: if sparks from the weld zone can reach the finish zone's paints, solvents, or wood, re-separate before the next job.
Stop: a one-person flow that starts taking structural or load-bearing work needs the same certified-welder rule — layout doesn't change qualification.

title: Keep a personal weld log: settings, results, lessons
mechanism_check: Memory lies about settings: the log remembers the amps, wire speed, and gas flow that actually worked.
A log turns every job into training data — patterns emerge: which rod, which thickness, which fix.
Career growth is visible in the log: six months of entries is a portfolio and a resume.
improvised_tools: A notebook at the welder or a notes app — the best log is the one you'll actually open.
A phone camera: one photo of the bead per setting is worth a page of notes.
A simple template: date, material, thickness, process, settings, result, lesson.
steps: Log every new combination the first time you run it — material, thickness, rod or wire, amps, result.
Photograph good beads and bad ones; label what was different.
Review the log before repeat jobs instead of re-guessing settings.
Note every defect and its fix — the fix column is the valuable part.
Bring the log to job interviews and certification tests — it proves the hours.
stop_conditions: PPE: logging happens cold and clean — never reach for the notebook with gloves that just handled hot metal.
Stop: a log of pretty beads on scrap is not qualification — load-bearing work still needs a certified welder and inspection.
Stop: if you're logging the same defect three times, stop and get coaching — the log is telling you something.

title: Price a small fab job: materials, time, and margin
mechanism_check: Small fab jobs lose money on time, not material: the steel is priced, the three hours of fit-up aren't.
Pricing is material cost plus consumables plus hours times rate plus margin — miss one term and you work for free.
Underpricing trains customers to expect it; the second job at a real price feels like a raise they didn't approve.
improvised_tools: A price sheet: your hourly rate, common material costs per foot, consumable estimates.
A timer or phone to track actual hours on the first few jobs — estimates need calibration.
A written quote template: scope, materials, timeline, price, what's excluded.
steps: Break the job into cut, fit, weld, finish; estimate hours per stage from your log, not optimism.
Price materials at retail plus 10% waste; add consumables (rod, wire, gas, discs).
Multiply hours by your rate; add 15-20% margin for the surprises every fab job hides.
Write the quote with scope and exclusions — 'brackets, not installation' prevents free work.
Track actual vs estimated hours and update your rates quarterly.
stop_conditions: PPE: pricing doesn't change the shop rules — every job still runs full PPE and fire watch.
Stop: never quote structural, load-bearing, or safety-critical work you aren't certified for — refer it out instead of pricing it.
Stop: if the customer wants it cheaper by skipping prep or inspection, walk away — cheap and unsafe is a liability, not a discount.

title: Fit-up mastery: cope tube joints with no notcher
mechanism_check: A coped joint is a saddle: the tube end is cut to hug the mating tube, giving full weld contact instead of a gap.
The cope profile is geometry: wrap a paper template of the intersection curve around the tube and cut to the line.
Tight cope means a strong, good-looking weld; gapped cope means a weld full of filler and weakness.
improvised_tools: Paper or thin cardboard for wrap-around templates.
A compass or contour gauge to capture the curve; a grinder or files to cut the cope.
A hole saw in a drill as a poor-man's notcher for common angles.
steps: Mark the intersection angle and tube diameters; draw the cope profile on paper.
Wrap the template on the tube end, aligning the centerline marks.
Cut proud of the line with a grinder or saw, then file to the line.
Test-fit against the mating tube — light should not show through the joint.
Tack at four points, check alignment, then weld; a good cope needs minimal filler.
stop_conditions: PPE: full grinding and arc PPE; coping throws sharp chips and the test-fit edges are knife-sharp.
Stop: coped joints in roll cages, handrails, or structural frames need certified welds and inspection — fit-up mastery doesn't replace qualification.
Stop: if the cope gaps exceed 1.5 mm, re-cut — bridging big gaps with weld metal is not a structural joint.

title: Crew play: two-person heavy lift and position
mechanism_check: Heavy steel injures backs and crushes hands when one person improvises the lift; two people with a plan move it safely.
The coordination challenge is timing: both lift, both set down, nobody's fingers under the steel at the moment of truth.
A lift plan spoken aloud beats a lift assumed — assumptions drop steel.
improvised_tools: Roles: a designated caller who counts the lift — everyone else moves on the caller's count.
Levers, rollers, and sawhorses staged before the lift so the steel has somewhere to go.
Gloves for everyone; steel-toe boots where the steel could land.
steps: Caller states the plan: path clear, destination ready, lift on three.
Both lifters grip, caller counts, steel rises together — no hero lifts.
Move in step to the destination; caller calls every set-down before it happens.
Fingers never under the steel; use the levers for final positioning.
Debrief in ten seconds: what was awkward becomes tomorrow's better plan.
stop_conditions: PPE: gloves and boots for everyone in the lift; nobody bare-handed under steel.
Stop: if anyone says stop, everything stops — the stop word outranks the caller.
Stop: loads over 50 kg per person or anything overhead need mechanical lifting (hoist, crane, forklift) — backs are not load-bearing equipment.

title: Crew play: tack-and-weld relay on a long frame
mechanism_check: Long frames warp when one welder runs one side continuously; alternating welders on opposite sides balances the heat.
The coordination challenge is sequence discipline: everyone welds their segment in the agreed order, no freelancing.
A relay turns a two-hour warp risk into a controlled, checkable process.
improvised_tools: Roles: a sequence caller plus welders assigned to stations — written on the whiteboard, not memorized.
A shared straightedge and square passed between stations for checks.
Chalk marks numbering each weld segment in sequence.
steps: Tack the full frame together as a crew; verify square and diagonals as a group.
Caller assigns segments: welder A takes odd segments on one side, welder B takes even on the other.
Weld one segment at a time, alternating sides; check square after every full round.
No one re-welds another's segment without telling the caller — sequence is the process.
Final group check: square, flat, all segments complete before anyone grinds.
stop_conditions: PPE: full arc PPE for every welder; bystanders and the sequence caller stay behind screens.
Stop: if the frame moves out of square mid-relay, stop the relay — cut tacks and re-fit rather than welding the warp in.
Stop: relay speed never overrides weld quality on load-bearing frames — those need a certified welder and inspection regardless of crew size.

title: Crew play: hot-work fire watch rotation
mechanism_check: Sparks smolder invisibly for up to an hour; a fire watch who leaves early is the same as no fire watch.
The coordination challenge is handoff: the watch is a continuous role, not a person — it must be explicitly passed, never assumed.
Rotation prevents watch fatigue: a fresh watcher actually watches.
improvised_tools: Roles: a named fire watcher per shift, written on the board — 'watch: Marcus 2-3pm, Priya 3-4pm'.
An extinguisher, a water bucket, and a phone at the watch station.
A 30-to-60-minute post-work timer that belongs to the watch role, not the welder.
steps: Before hot work starts, name the first watcher and the rotation order out loud.
The watcher stays in the area with eyes on the work zone — phone down, watching.
Handoff is verbal and explicit: 'I have the watch' / 'You have the watch' — both confirm.
After welding stops, the watch continues 30-60 minutes; the timer doesn't start until the last spark.
The final watcher signs off that the area is cold before anyone leaves.
stop_conditions: PPE: the watcher wears eye protection and keeps a clear path to the extinguisher.
Stop: if the rotation breaks down and no one holds the watch, stop all hot work until it's re-established.
Stop: a fire watch is not a firefighter — if it ignites beyond a bucket of water, evacuate and call emergency services.
Stop: the fire watch covers fire risk, not weld qualification — load-bearing welds made on the job still need a certified welder and inspection.

title: Crew play: shift handoff that passes the job state, not just the torch
mechanism_check: Most crew mistakes happen at handoff: the next shift re-welds finished joints or misses the one joint that failed inspection.
The coordination challenge is state transfer: what's done, what's half-done, what's wrong — in that order.
A five-minute handoff prevents a five-hour rework.
improvised_tools: A handoff board or log: done / in-progress / blocked, updated at every shift end.
Chalk or paint marks on the work itself: finished welds marked, defects circled.
The outgoing lead walks the incoming lead through the work — never a note left on a bench.
steps: Outgoing lead updates the board: what's welded, what's tacked, what's waiting on material or inspection.
Walk the work together; point at every in-progress joint and every known defect.
State the settings in use — rod, amps, gas — so the next shift doesn't re-guess.
Flag anything hot, anything under clamp, anything not to touch.
Incoming lead repeats back the blocked items; both sign the handoff.
stop_conditions: PPE: handoff walks happen cold — verify no one is about to strike an arc during the walkthrough.
Stop: if the outgoing crew can't account for a joint's state, mark it unknown and re-inspect — never assume it.
Stop: load-bearing welds awaiting inspection stay flagged until a certified inspector signs — the handoff doesn't clear them.

title: Crew play: improvise a briefing when the plan changes mid-job
mechanism_check: Plans change mid-job: material is wrong, a joint won't fit, the customer adds scope — the crew keeps working from the old plan unless someone stops it.
The coordination challenge is the pause: stopping a moving crew feels costly, but working from a dead plan costs more.
A two-minute huddle re-syncs faster than any amount of shouting across the shop.
improvised_tools: A ritual: anyone can call 'huddle' and all work stops — the word outranks momentum.
The whiteboard or the work itself as the shared reference — point, don't describe.
Roles re-assigned on the spot: who does what under the new plan, said out loud.
steps: Whoever spots the change calls 'huddle' — all hot work stops, hoods up.
State the change plainly: what broke, what's different, what the customer actually needs now.
Re-plan on the board: new sequence, new assignments, new risks — two minutes, not twenty.
Everyone confirms their new task out loud; the caller confirms the safety changes.
Resume only when the caller says go — the huddle ends with a decision, not a drift.
stop_conditions: PPE: huddle happens with hoods up and grinders down — the pause is total.
Stop: if the change affects structural or load-bearing scope, stop and get engineering or certified review before re-planning — the crew doesn't redesign structure on the fly.
Stop: if anyone is unclear on their new task after the huddle, re-brief that person — confusion is how injuries happen.

title: Train the new hire on the grinder before the welder
mechanism_check: The grinder injures more shop workers than the welder: kickback, burst wheels, and sparks are less respected than the arc.
The coordination challenge is sequencing: new hires want the welder, but the grinder is what they'll use most and fear least.
Grinder competence first makes every later welding lesson safer — prep and cleanup are half the trade.
improvised_tools: A dedicated training station with scrap, a guarded grinder, and a face shield that stays there.
A progression card: guard check, disc check, stance, flat grinding, edge work — signed off step by step.
A mentor assigned for the first week, not whoever happens to be free.
steps: Day one: guard on, disc rated above RPM, stance to the side, two hands — drill it before any grinding.
Practice on scrap: flat passes, then edges, then weld blending — mentor watches every pass.
Teach the sounds: a chattering disc is a failing disc — stop and change it.
Sign off each step on the progression card; no skipping to welding until grinding is solid.
Pair the new hire with the mentor on real cleanup work before any arc time.
stop_conditions: PPE: face shield over glasses, gloves, respirator, hearing protection — the full grinder kit, no exceptions, from the first minute.
Stop: a grinder with a missing guard or a cracked disc is a lockout — tag it and take it out of service.
Stop: new hires don't touch structural weld prep or load-bearing grinding until signed off — the card gates the work.
